title: If Romans call dead faith justifying, they mean remote disposition only
source_text: LI. Quod si nonnulli Scholae Romanae Theologi justificantis nomen quandoque ipsi fidei mortuae & otiosae attribuunt, per id non significant illam actu justificare, sed solum illam ad justificationem non proxime, sed remote disponere. In hac autem quaestione Reformati non agunt de remota quadam dispositione, nec multum laborant, An fides etiam mortua sit istiusmodi quaedam ad justificationem remota dispositio. Sed id solum docere & asserere intendunt, nullam aliam fidem quam vivam atque efficacem homines ad justificationem infallibiliter & proxime disponere: qua in re assentientes habent Scholae Romanae Theologos.
pass_a_gloss: But if some theologians of the Roman school sometimes attribute the name justifying even to dead and idle faith itself, by that they do not signify that it actually justifies, but only that it disposes to justification not proximately but remotely. In this question, however, the Reformed are not dealing with some remote disposition, nor do they labor much whether even dead faith is such a remote disposition to justification. But they intend only to teach and assert that no faith other than living and efficacious disposes people infallibly and proximately to justification — in which matter they have the theologians of the Roman school agreeing.
pass_b_english: When some Romans label dead idle faith justifying, they mean remote disposition, not actual justification.
Reformed press only that living efficacious faith disposes infallibly and proximately — and Rome agrees on that point.

lemmas.gloss: to dispose not proximately but remotely

choices.why: Justifying name on dead faith = remote only.
